newsitem.title: UK: UK election fever fades after Major wins key vote.
newsitem.headline: UK election fever fades after Major wins key vote.

text.p: Speculation that Prime Minister John Major would be forced to call an early election died down on Tuesday after his government survived a parliamentary vote over its handling of the crisis over mad cow disease.

The motion, criticising Agriculture Minister Douglas Hogg for his handling of the crisis and demanding his salary be cut, was rejected in the lower House of Commons by 320 votes to 307 on Monday night.
Tony Blair, leader of the main opposiiton Labour party which called the vote, claimed a moral victory and said Monday's debate had exposed the huge cost to taxpayers of the crisis.

"Between now and the general election, since the government are delaying it, we will expose not just what they've done on beef but what they are doing on health, jobs, on crime, on education and a whole range of issues," Blair told reporters.
His deputy added that Labour was not giving up the fight to bring the government down ahead of the May 22 election deadline.
"We are concentrating all our efforts to get rid of this government at any opportunity," Labour deputy leader John Prescott told BBC radio.
The government has 322 seats in the Commons, the same number as all the other parties combined.

Labour, enjoying an opinion poll lead of around 20 points, needed to win the support of all the other opposition parties -- plus at least one rebel from the ruling Conservatives -- to defeat the government in Monday night's vote.
A government defeat would have triggered a vote of confidence that could have forced Major to hold a snap election instead of soldiering on until May 1, his preferred date.

But in the hours leading up to the vote, the government enticed the nine members of the Ulster Unionist party, which represents Northern Ireland's pro-British Protestant majority, with offers of special help for their farmers. The nine then abstained.

Major is expected to be pushed into a minority if Labour wins a by-election on February 27 in the Wirral South seat in north-west England. Opinion polls show Labour will win a seat taken by a Conservative at the 1992 general election.
Prescott said a Labour victory could prompt a fresh attempt to bring the government down when a good opportunity presented itself.
"If we win that by-election we will assess it... We have always made it absolutely clear that we will take every opportunity but... let us wait and see what happens," he said.
The government is sensitive to attacks on its handling of the mad cow crisis, which Hogg admitted on Monday had cost the country 3.5 billion pounds ($5.67 billion) so far.

The EU imposed a worldwide ban on British beef exports last March because of evidence mad cow disease, or bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE), could be transmitted to humans with fatal results. ($1=.6173 Pound)
